title: Short Stuff: White Dog Poop
summary: Short Stuff episode on why white dog poop was common in the 1980s and largely disappeared. Josh and Chuck attribute it to excess calcium from bone meal and rendered bones in standard dog food of the 1960s through 1980s, which dogs could not fully absorb; the calcium passed in feces and dried chalky white. They trace dog food history from post-World War Two extruded fillers and horse meat through improvements in the late 1980s and 1990s and more recent grain-free and real-food diets. They also cover what healthy dog poop looks like and what colors (white speckled, orange, yellow, green, gray, red, black tarry) may signal. Personal dog anecdotes and a note about Chuck's aging dog Charlie are included, plus sponsor reads.

segments.title: Opening banter and the white dog poop mystery
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck introduce the topic of white dog poop, referencing a Sarah Silverman bit and the Stepbrothers scene, and reminisce about dogs they owned in the 1980s whose poop did not come out white.

segments.title: Calcium explanation for white dog poop
segments.summary: Chuck and Josh explain that 1980s dog food was loaded with bone meal and bones, giving dogs excess calcium they could not absorb. The calcium passed in feces and dried chalky white in the sun. Poor rendering of bones made absorption even harder.

segments.title: Hosts' childhood dogs
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck share personal stories about their dogs from the 1980s, including a dog that rescued a schnauzer from the pool and a family dog that Chuck's parents kept outdoors.

segments.title: Mid-episode break
segments.summary: Chuck transitions to a promised discussion of dog food after a break.

segments.title: Dog food history after World War Two
segments.summary: The hosts describe how dog food was made cheaply after World War Two, including horse meat earlier in the century, extrusion that removed nutrients, cheap fillers, and high calcium. Manufacturers' push for profit is contrasted with later improvements.

segments.title: Improvement in dog food in late 1980s and 1990s
segments.summary: Josh explains that consumer pressure and industry change in the late 1980s and 1990s lowered calcium levels, which made white dog poop disappear. The hosts note that dog food has since become healthier, though debates remain over vegan diets and wet versus dry food.

segments.title: Grain-free diets and fat sensitivity in dogs
segments.summary: Chuck describes his dogs' move to grain-free diets for autoimmune issues. Josh notes grain can be hard on some dogs and that excess fat can cause pancreatitis or gastritis.

segments.title: What dog poop colors mean
segments.summary: The hosts describe healthy dog stool as firm, chocolatey brown tube. They explain that speckled white can indicate worms, old-school white suggests high calcium or ground-bone raw diets, and orange, yellow, green, gray, red, and black tarry stool each signal different digestive issues.

segments.title: Chuck's aging dog and incontinence
segments.summary: Chuck talks about cleaning up after his fourteen-year-old dog Charlie, who has become incontinent due to stiff back legs and aging.

segments.title: Sponsor thanks and KSNF listener note
segments.summary: The hosts thank sponsors IFL Science, All Dogs Poop, and KSNF of Joplin, Missouri, which provided information for the episode, and close with a short joke.
